actions.justification: Mandatory first step for upper GI bleed - patient has tachycardia (HR 105) suggesting possible hemodynamic compromise. Must assess volume status and stability.
Mandatory initial assessment to fully characterize hemodynamic stability in the setting of acute upper GI bleed with hematemesis and melena.
Mandatory - large-bore IV access required immediately for fluid resuscitation and potential blood product administration in upper GI bleed.
★ MANDATORY: CBC is essential to assess hemoglobin/hematocrit levels in the setting of active upper GI bleeding (hematemesis and melena). Guides transfusion decisions.
★ MANDATORY: Coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT) are critical in upper GI bleed to identify coagulopathy that may be contributing to or complicating the bleed, and to guide management.
★ MANDATORY: Type and crossmatch is required to prepare packed red blood cells for potential transfusion given active upper GI hemorrhage with hemodynamic instability (HR 105, MAP 73).

BMP provides BUN/creatinine ratio (elevated in UGIB due to blood digestion and absorption), electrolytes, and renal function, which are essential for risk stratification and management in upper GI bleeding.
Patient has HR 105 suggesting hypovolemia from GI blood loss. IV crystalloid bolus provides volume resuscitation to maintain hemodynamic stability while awaiting packed RBCs if needed.

Empiric IV proton pump inhibitor is indicated in suspected upper GI bleeding (hematemesis/melena) to reduce acid secretion, stabilize clots, and decrease rebleeding risk prior to endoscopy per standard UGIB guidelines.

GI consultation is essential for a patient with hematemesis and melena to arrange urgent upper endoscopy for diagnosis and potential therapeutic intervention (hemostasis). This is a standard of care action for upper GI bleeding.
Lactate level helps assess tissue perfusion and severity of bleeding. HR 105 suggests possible compensated shock; lactate will guide resuscitation adequacy.
Type and crossmatch (beyond the already completed type and screen) is needed to prepare packed RBCs for potential transfusion given active GI bleeding with tachycardia.

Prokinetic agent (e.g., erythromycin or metoclopramide) given before endoscopy improves gastric visualization by promoting gastric emptying, which is standard of care in upper GI bleeding with hematemesis.

Octreotide (somatostatin analogue) reduces splanchnic blood flow and portal pressure, indicated empirically in upper GI bleeding to reduce bleeding, particularly if variceal etiology is possible given hematemesis and melena.

Repeat CBC to trend hemoglobin and hematocrit as initial labs are still pending; serial monitoring is essential to guide transfusion decisions (transfuse if Hgb < 7 g/dL) and assess ongoing blood loss in this tachycardic patient.
Repeat CBC to assess hemoglobin level and guide transfusion decision; initial CBC is still pending and patient is tachycardic with active GI bleeding.
Repeat lactate to evaluate tissue perfusion and severity of hemorrhagic shock given ongoing tachycardia (HR 105) despite fluid resuscitation.
Surgical consult indicated for significant upper GI bleeding (hematemesis + melena) in case endoscopic therapy fails or surgical intervention is needed.

Patient with hematemesis and melena has pending CBC. Transfusion threshold of Hgb <7 is standard of care for upper GI bleed per guidelines. Ordering now so it can be administered immediately once CBC results return, given tachycardia (HR 105) suggesting hemodynamic compromise.
CT abdomen can help identify the source and extent of GI bleeding, assess for vascular abnormalities, or identify other etiologies of the bleeding prior to or in planning for endoscopy/intervention.

Patient with hematemesis and melena has had initial stabilization measures completed. Angiography can help localize the source of GI bleeding and may allow for therapeutic intervention (embolization) if endoscopy is not immediately available or has failed to control bleeding. With HR 105 and ongoing bleeding concern, identifying the bleeding source is clinically indicated.
Monitoring urine output is essential in this GI bleed patient to assess end-organ perfusion and adequacy of fluid resuscitation, particularly given ongoing tachycardia.
CBC, coagulation studies, BMP, and lactate are all pending. Reviewing results as they return will guide transfusion decisions, coagulopathy correction, and further management of this upper GI bleed.
